claim: All life on our planet requires ribonucleotide reduction for de novo synthesis of deoxyribonucleotides from ribonucleotides.
source: All life on our planet requires ribonucleotide reduction for de novo synthesis of deoxyribonucleotides, from ribonucleotides (Nordlund and Reichard, 2006; Lundin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Nordlund and Reichard, 2006; Lundin et al., 2009).

claim: The emergence of ribonucleotide reduction likely drove the transition from RNA to DNA early in the evolution of life.
source: The emergence of ribonucleotide reduction likely drove the transition from RNA to DNA early in the evolution of life (Lundin et al., 2015; Reichard, 1993; Torrents et al., 2002; Poole et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The centrality of ribonucleotide reduction is reflected in its near ubiquity in organismal genomes.
source: its centrality is reflected in its near ubiquity in organismal genomes (Lundin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Lundin et al., 2009).

claim: The catalytic cores of ribonucleotide reductases (RNRs) are homologous.
source: Structural analyses indicate that the catalytic cores of ribonucleotide reductases (RNRs) are homologous (Lundin et al., 2015; Sintchak et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to structural analyses in published literature.

claim: Sequence similarities between RNRs are extremely limited despite their homologous catalytic cores.
source: despite sequence similarities between them being extremely limited (Tauer and Benner, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Tauer and Benner, 1997).

claim: RNRs catalyse deoxyribonucleotide synthesis via a common mechanism wherein a cysteinyl-free radical is generated in the active site.
source: RNRs catalyse deoxyribonucleotide synthesis via a common mechanism wherein a cysteinyl-free radical is generated in the active site.
evidence: The claim is presented as established knowledge about RNR mechanism.

claim: RNRs have diverse mechanisms for radical generation.
source: RNRs have diverse mechanisms for radical generation (Nordlund and Reichard, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Three broad, evolutionarily distinct, families of RNRs exist which are divided on the basis of their radical generation mechanism.
source: Three broad, evolutionarily distinct, families exist which are also divided on the basis of their radical generation mechanism (Nordlund and Reichard, 2006; Lundin et al., 2015; Lundin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The divergence of RNR families likely coincides with adaptation to varied environments.
source: This divergence likely coincides with adaptation to varied environments (Lundin et al., 2010; Hofer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Class I RNR enzymes are strictly aerobic in that they require oxygen or superoxide for activation.
source: Class I enzymes are strictly aerobic in that they require oxygen or superoxide for activation (Rose et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Class III RNR enzymes generate a stable glycine radical via cleavage of S-adenosyl methionine and are strictly anaerobic.
source: Class III enzymes generate a stable glycine radical via cleavage of S-adenosyl methionine, and are strictly anaerobic
evidence: The claim is presented as established knowledge about Class III RNRs.

claim: Class II RNR enzymes generate a 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical through cleavage of adenosylcobalamin and operate irrespective of oxygen presence or absence.
source: class II enzymes generate a 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical through cleavage of adenosylcobalamin and operate irrespective of oxygen presence or absence.
evidence: The claim is presented as established knowledge about Class II RNRs.

claim: Very few species have dispensed with ribonucleotide reduction by relying on their hosts for deoxyribonucleotides.
source: To date, very few species have dispensed with ribonucleotide reduction, albeit indirectly, in that they instead rely on their hosts for deoxyribonucleotides (Lundin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Buchnera aphidicola str. Cc from the Cedar bark aphid lacks ribonucleotide reduction.
source: Examples include a strain of Buchnera aphidicola str. Cc from the Cedar bark aphid, Cinara cedri (Pérez-Brocal et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: B. aphidicola are maternally inherited aphid endosymbionts that synthesise amino acids in short supply in the aphid diet.
source: B. aphidicola are maternally inherited aphid endosymbionts that synthesise amino acids in short supply in the aphid diet, are obligately intracellular, and appear to be on the path to transitioning to an organelle (Andersson, 2000; Tamas et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ureaplasma urealyticum has lost genes for ribonucleotide reduction.
source: Two bacterial pathogens that live in very close association with their hosts—Ureaplasma urealyticum (Glass et al., 2000) and Borrelia burgdorferi (Fraser et al., 1997)—have also lost genes for ribonucleotide reduction
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Borrelia burgdorferi has lost genes for ribonucleotide reduction.
source: Two bacterial pathogens that live in very close association with their hosts—Ureaplasma urealyticum (Glass et al., 2000) and Borrelia burgdorferi (Fraser et al., 1997)—have also lost genes for ribonucleotide reduction
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Giardia lamblia and Entamoeba histolytica have lost ribonucleotide reduction.
source: as have two eukaryotic parasites, Giardia lamblia and Entamoeba histolytica (Lundin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The authors successfully eliminated all three RNR operons from Escherichia coli.
source: We report the successful elimination of all three RNR operons from the bacterium Escherichia coli.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including PCR, RT-PCR, and whole genome sequencing results shown in Figure 1.

claim: The knockout strain was created by introducing a broad-spectrum deoxyribonucleoside kinase from Mycoplasma mycoides.
source: The knockout strain was created by introducing a broad-spectrum deoxyribonucleoside kinase from Mycoplasma mycoides (Wang et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to published literature about the kinase.

claim: The ΔRNR strain is dependent on deoxyribonucleosides in the growth medium.
source: As predicted, the resulting strain is dependent on deoxyribonucleosides in the growth medium
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The ΔRNR strain cannot grow if the media are supplemented with deoxyribose (dR) plus the four nucleobases (A, G, C, T).
source: but cannot grow if the media are supplemented with deoxyribose (dR) plus the four nucleobases (A, G, C, T).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The DERA pathway is reversible in vitro.
source: This pathway is reversible in vitro (Horinouchi et al., 2006a; Ogawa et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The DERA pathway has long been considered a plausible alternative to ribonucleotide reduction for dNTP synthesis.
source: and has long been considered a plausible alternative to ribonucleotide reduction (Racker, 1951; Racker, 1952) for dNTP synthesis
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The DERA pathway is not coopted for deoxyribonucleotide synthesis following loss of ribonucleotide reduction.
source: Our evolution experiments reveal that this pathway is not coopted for deoxyribonucleotide synthesis following loss of ribonucleotide reduction
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental evolution data and genome sequencing results showing mutations in deoB rather than adaptation of the DERA pathway for synthesis.

claim: Cells grown under limiting deoxyribonucleoside levels exhibit a filamentous cell morphology indicative of stress.
source: with cells grown under limiting deoxyribonucleoside levels exhibiting a filamentous morphology indicative of stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in deoB are predicted to prevent catabolism of 2-deoxy-D-ribose-1-phosphate.
source: we observe loss-of-function mutations in deoB, which are predicted to prevent catabolism of 2-deoxy-D-ribose-1-phosphate.
evidence: The claim is based on genome sequencing data and inference from the known function of deoB.

claim: A 25-fold reduction in the minimum concentration of exogenous deoxyribonucleosides necessary for growth was observed over the course of the evolution experiment.
source: Over the course of an evolution experiment, we observe a 25-fold reduction in the minimum concentration of exogenous deoxyribonucleosides necessary for growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data comparing evolved lines to ancestral lines at different deoxyribonucleoside concentrations.

claim: Several replicate lines carry mutations in deoB and cdd.
source: Genome analysis reveals that several replicate lines carry mutations in deoB and cdd.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data of evolved lines.

claim: deoB codes for phosphopentomutase, a key part of the deoxyriboaldolase pathway.
source: deoB codes for phosphopentomutase, a key part of the deoxyriboaldolase pathway
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of gene function.

claim: Mutations in deoB reduce or eliminate the capacity for the DERA pathway to catabolise deoxyribonucleotides, preventing their loss via central metabolism.
source: our experiments reveal that mutations appear that reduce or eliminate the capacity for this pathway to catabolise deoxyribonucleotides, thus preventing their loss via central metabolism.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing mutations in deoB and understanding of the pathway's function.

claim: Mutational inactivation of both deoB and cdd is observed in a number of obligate intracellular bacteria that have lost ribonucleotide reduction.
source: Mutational inactivation of both deoB and cdd is also observed in a number of obligate intracellular bacteria that have lost ribonucleotide reduction.
evidence: The claim is supported by genome database searches and analysis of bacterial genomes presented in the manuscript.

claim: The experiments recapitulate key evolutionary steps in the adaptation to life without ribonucleotide reduction.
source: We conclude that our experiments recapitulate key evolutionary steps in the adaptation to life without ribonucleotide reduction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental evolution data and comparison with natural bacterial genomes.

claim: E. coli carries genes for three RNRs: aerobic class Ia (nrdAB operon), class Ib (nrdHIEF), and anaerobic class III (nrdDG).
source: E. coli carries genes for three RNRs: aerobic class Ia (encoded by the nrdAB operon), class Ib (nrdHIEF), and anaerobic class III (nrdDG) (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Under aerobic growth, ribonucleotide reduction is primarily performed by the iron-dependent class Ia enzyme.
source: Under aerobic growth, ribonucleotide reduction is primarily performed by the iron-dependent class Ia enzyme (Monje-Casas et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Class Ib RNR has a manganese metal centre.
source: while class Ib has a manganese metal centre (Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Class Ib RNR is able to support growth when iron is scarce.
source: and is therefore able to support growth when iron is scarce (Martin and Imlay, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: All three RNR operons were successfully deleted from the ΔRNR line as confirmed by PCR.
source: Our results indicate that all three operons were successfully deleted (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Whole genome sequencing confirmed deletion of all genes for ribonucleotide reduction in the ΔRNR line.
source: Finally, knockout status was confirmed with whole genome sequencing. This confirmed deletion of all genes for ribonucleotide reduction
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: The nrdAB operon was successfully deleted under heterologous expression of dAK from M. mycoides.
source: with the nrdAB operon successfully deleted under heterologous expression of dAK from M. mycoides (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data including RT-PCR shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Genome sequencing revealed 23 SNPs that likely appeared during the creation of ΔRNR from wild-type progenitor line (REL606).
source: In addition to lacking all nrd genes, genome sequencing revealed 23 SNPs that likely appeared during the creation of ΔRNR from wild-type progenitor line (REL606) (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: At high dN concentrations (1 mg/mL), ΔRNR grows favourably, though shows a clear lag compared to wild-type on equivalent media.
source: At high dN concentrations (1 mg/mL), ΔRNR grows favourably, though shows a clear lag compared to wild-type on equivalent media (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At lower dN concentrations, ΔRNR growth is impaired, but there is still discernible growth at 0.05 mg/mL.
source: At lower dN concentrations, ΔRNR growth is impaired, but there is still discernible growth at 0.05 mg/mL (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At 0.01 mg/mL dN concentration, only marginal growth of ΔRNR was observed.
source: When this is dropped to 0.01 mg/mL we observed only marginal growth of ΔRNR (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the absence of dN supplementation no growth of ΔRNR is observed, while wild-type lines are unaffected.
source: As expected, in the absence of dN supplementation no growth is observed, while wild-type lines are unaffected (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: No growth of ΔRNR was observed when grown on dR plus the four bases (A, G, C, T).
source: Finally, we tried growing ΔRNR on dR plus the four bases (A, G, C, T). No growth was observed (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Deletion of the three nrd operons from ΔRNR has completely eliminated the capacity for de novo deoxyribonucleotide synthesis.
source: These results indicate that deletion of the three nrd operons from ΔRNR has completely eliminated the capacity for de novo deoxyribonucleotide synthesis; no other genes appear able to compensate for this deficiency.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from growth assay data showing complete dependence on exogenous deoxyribonucleosides.

claim: ΔRNR is unable to grow in the presence of dA, dG, or dT alone or in combination.
source: This revealed that ΔRNR is unable to grow in the presence of dA, dG, or dT (either alone [Figure 3A–C] or in combination [Figure 3E]), even after 44 hr of monitoring (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3A-C and 3E.

claim: ΔRNR can grow on dC alone.
source: However, ΔRNR can grow on dC alone (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: dC is the sole dN required for ΔRNR growth in minimal media.
source: Together these data indicate dC is the sole dN required for ΔRNR growth in minimal media.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from growth assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ΔRNR cells are elongated and filamentous at very low levels of dNs.
source: Examination of cells at ×100 magnification revealed that ΔRNR cells are elongated and filamentous at very low levels of dNs, whereas ΔRNR cells have a similar morphology to wild-type at higher dN concentrations (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Some ΔRNR cells reached lengths several times that of wild-type.
source: Some cells reached lengths several times that of wild-type (Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell length measurement data.

claim: The filamentous phenotype of ΔRNR is environmental and can be reversed if cells are moved to a high [dN] environment.
source: This demonstrates that the phenotype is environmental and can be reversed if cells are moved to a high [dN] environment.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C demonstrating phenotype reversal upon transfer to high dN concentration.

claim: ΔRNR cells grown in low [dN] contain multiple DAPI-stained regions across the length of the cells, suggestive of multiple DNA nucleoids.
source: This revealed the presence of multiple DAPI-stained regions across the length of the cells (Figure 4B), suggestive of the presence of multiple DNA nucleoids in ΔRNR cells grown at low [dN].
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At the beginning of the evolution experiment, ∆RNR cells are substantially longer than wild-type, particularly at 0.25 mg/mL dNs.
source: At the beginning of the experiment, ∆RNR cells are substantially longer than wild-type, particularly at 0.25 mg/mL dNs (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell length measurement data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Cell lengths of 20 μM were recorded at 0.25 mg/mL dNs (average of 6 μM), which is 10–20 times the length of wild-type cells.
source: We recorded cell lengths of 20 μM at this lower concentration (average of 6 μM), a staggering 10–20 times the length of wild-type cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell length measurement data.

claim: By transfer 30, average cell length of evolved ΔRNR lines was comparable to wild-type at both dN concentrations.
source: By the time the experiment had reached 30 transfers, average cell length was comparable to wild-type at both dN concentrations (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell length measurement data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: All five ∆RNR lines evolved at 1 mg/mL dNs (∆RNR1000_T30_L1–5) showed improved growth relative to ∆RNR_T0 at 1 mg/mL.
source: At 1 mg/mL, ∆RNR1000_T30_L1 through L5 all showed improved growth relative to ∆RNR_T0 (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: All evolved lines (∆RNR1000_T30_L1–5) showed improved growth at 0.01 mg/mL dNs compared to ∆RNR_T0.
source: Moreover, compared to ∆RNR_T0, which exhibited almost no growth at 0.01 mg/mL dNs (Figure 2D), all evolved lines (∆RNR1000_T30_L1–5) showed improved growth at this low concentration (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Elongate cell morphology and clumping preclude use of OD measurements for accurate estimation of doubling time or cell counts.
source: Note however that elongate cell morphology and clumping preclude use of OD measurements for accurate estimation of doubling time or cell counts (Stevenson et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge cited from published literature.

claim: All evolved lines failed to grow in the absence of dN supplementation, indicating they remain reliant on media supplementation.
source: All lines failed to grow in the absence of dN supplementation (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), indicating they remain reliant on media supplementation.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Evolved knockout lines (∆RNR250_T30_L1–5 and ∆RNR1000_T30_L1–5) all accumulated substantially more mutations than wild-type controls evolved at the same dN concentration.
source: Our evolved knockout lines (∆RNR250_T30_L1–5 and ∆RNR1000_T30_L1–5) all accumulated substantially more mutations than wild-type controls evolved at the same dN concentration (Figure 8, Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 8 and Supplementary file 1E.

claim: ∆RNR250_T30 lines accumulated the greatest numbers of mutations (range: 39–118 SNPs).
source: Our ∆RNR250_T30 lines accumulated the greatest numbers of mutations (range: 39–118 SNPs).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: ∆RNR1000_T30 lines exhibited a small but significant increase in total SNPs relative to wild-type (p=0.01, unpaired t-test).
source: ∆RNR1000_T30 lines did exhibit a small but significant increase in total SNPs relative to wild-type (Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1E; p=0.01, unpaired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data and statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in total mutations between wild-type lines evolved in either 1 mg/mL or 0.25 mg/mL dNs (p=0.10; unpaired t-test).
source: There was no significant difference in total mutations between wild-type lines evolved in either 1 mg/mL or 0.25 mg/mL dNs (p=0.10; unpaired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data and statistical analysis.

claim: 88% of SNPs in ∆RNR250_T30 lines are A:T→G:C substitutions.
source: Indeed, 88% of SNPs in our ∆RNR250_T30 lines are of one type: A:T→G:C (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 8.

claim: One gene, cdd, which codes for cytidine deaminase, was mutated in 8 of 10 lines from transfer 30.
source: Analysis of our genome data from lines at transfer 30 revealed that one gene, cdd, which codes for cytidine deaminase, was mutated in 8 of 10 lines from transfer 30 (Supplementary file 1F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: Seven of eight lines with cdd mutations carried an identical deletion.
source: Analysis of the data revealed that seven of eight lines carried an identical deletion (Supplementary file 1F, G; Figure 8—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: One line possessed an SNP in cdd that was predicted to result in a truncation.
source: while one line possessed an SNP that was predicted to result in a truncation.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data and prediction based on the mutation's position.

claim: The glycerol stock used to establish the evolution experiments (∆RNR31) was a mixed population, with both intact and cdd deletion present.
source: This revealed that the glycerol stock that we used to establish our evolution experiments (∆RNR31) was a mixed population, with both intact and cdd deletion present (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR screening data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: After 30 transfers, all 10 lines (∆RNR_T30_1000_L1–5, ∆RNR_T30_250_L1–5) were polymorphic for the deleted cdd locus.
source: Moreover, it appears that, after 30 transfers, all 10 lines (∆RNR_T30_1000_L1–5, ∆RNR_T30_250_L1–5) were polymorphic for the deleted locus.
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR screening data.

claim: After two transfers, the emergence of a cdd deletion was observed in several replicate lines derived from ∆RNR34.
source: After two transfers, we observed the emergence of a cdd deletion in several replicate lines (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR screening data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: One gene, deoB, was mutated in eight lines at transfer 40.
source: One gene, deoB, was mutated in eight lines (Table 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data presented in Table 1.

claim: deoB codes for phosphopentomutase, which catalyses the transfer of a phosphate group between the C1 and C5 carbon atoms of deoxyribose.
source: and is particularly noteworthy in the context of our experiment in that it codes for phosphopentomutase. This enzyme catalyses the transfer of a phosphate group between the C1 and C5 carbon atoms of deoxribose
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of gene function.

claim: Phosphopentomutase is responsible for the committed step in deoxyribonucleotide salvage.
source: and is responsible for the committed step in deoxyribonucleotide salvage (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of the enzyme's role in the pathway.

claim: deoB has independently mutated five or six times under the conditions of the experiment.
source: Conservatively, it thus appears that deoB has independently mutated five or six times under the conditions of our experiment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genome sequencing data and analysis of shared mutations between lines.

claim: Three of the five unique mutations observed in deoB directly impact conserved active site residues, either through truncation or mutation of active site residues.
source: Of the five unique mutations observed in our experiment (Table 1), three directly impact conserved active site residues, either through truncation or mutation of active site residues (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis mapping mutations onto the B. cereus phosphopentomutase structure.

claim: All observed mutations to the deoB gene are likely to impact phosphopentomutase function, with some expected to completely inactivate the enzyme.
source: We therefore conclude that these mutations to the deoB gene are all likely to impact phosphopentomutase function, with some expected to completely inactivate the enzyme.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from structural analysis and sequence alignment data.

claim: Blastp searches confirmed absence of RNRs and phosphopentomutase in B. burgdorferi, U. urealyticum, and B. aphidicola str. Cc.
source: For the three specific species above, blastp searches (Supplementary file 1K) confirmed absence of RNRs and phosphopentomutase (encoded by deoB).
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST search results against genome databases.

claim: A hit to cytidine deaminase (encoded by cdd) was identified for B. burgdorferi.
source: A hit to cytidine deaminase (encoded by cdd) was identified for B. burgdorferi.
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST search results.

claim: With the possible exception of Candidatus Ureaplasma intestinipullorum, no members of the genus Ureaplasma carry genes for RNR, PPM, or CDD.
source: Thus, with the possible exception of Candidatus Ureaplasma intestinipullorum, no members of the genus Ureaplasma carry genes for RNR, PPM, or CDD.
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST searches against all Ureaplasma genome assemblies.

claim: The majority of Borrelia genome species code for class Ib RNR.
source: We screened 77 available genome assemblies, recovering 73 hits to NrdE and 67 to NrdF, indicating that the majority of Borrelia genome species code for class Ib RNR.
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST searches against Borrelia genome assemblies.

claim: Only one member of the Borreliella returned any hits to RNR: Candidatus Borreliella tachyglossi appears to have a class Ib RNR.
source: Only one member of the Borelliella returned any hits to RNR: Candidatus Borreliella tachyglossi appears to have a class Ib RNR (Supplementary file 1M).
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST searches against Borreliella genome assemblies.

claim: No members of either Borrelia or Borreliella carry deoB.
source: For all genome assemblies from both candidate genera, no significant hits to either PPM (deoB) or YohK were returned. These data indicate that no members of either Borrelia or Borreliella carry deoB
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST searches against genome assemblies.

claim: Only the Borreliella apparently lack ribonucleotide reduction.
source: with only the Borreliella apparently lacking ribonucleotide reduction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from BLAST search results showing RNR presence in Borrelia but absence in most Borreliella.

claim: Only one specific strain of B. aphidicola (from the cedar aphid C. cedri) lacked RNR genes.
source: Lundin et al., 2009, noted that only one specific strain of B. aphidicola (from the cedar aphid C. cedri) lacked RNR genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: B. aphidicola Str. Cc has no coding potential for RNR, PPMase, CDD, and YokH.
source: A search against B. aphidicola Str. Cc (taxid:372461) revealed no coding potential for RNR, PPMase, CDD, and YokH (Supplementary file 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST search results.

claim: Of 74 B. aphidicola assemblies, 22 strains lack both ribonucleotide reduction and phosphopentomutase coding.
source: Of 74 assemblies, we found 22 strains that lack both ribonucleotide reduction and phosphopentomutase coding
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST searches against B. aphidicola genome assemblies.

claim: Two B. aphidicola strains possess a deoB gene but lack genes for ribonucleotide reduction.
source: two strains that possess a deoB gene but lack genes for ribonucleotide reduction
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST searches against B. aphidicola genome assemblies.

claim: Two B. aphidicola strains possess genes for ribonucleotide reduction but lack deoB.
source: and two with the opposite pattern (Supplementary file 1N).
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST searches against B. aphidicola genome assemblies.

claim: The ∆RNR knockout line grows on MOPS minimal media + 1% glucose supplemented with dNs.
source: Our ∆RNR knockout line grows on MOPS minimal media + 1% glucose supplemented with dNs (Figure 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The ∆RNR knockout line does not grow when provided with dR and the four bases A, G, C, T.
source: but does not grow when provided with their constituent components (dR and the four bases A, G, C, T).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Of the four dNs, only dC is essential for growth of the ∆RNR line.
source: Growth experiments reveal that, of the four dNs, only dC is essential for growth (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Under limiting levels of dNs, the ∆RNR lines exhibit a filamentous phenotype that can be reversed by increasing dN supplementation.
source: Under limiting levels of dNs, our lines exhibit a filamentous phenotype that can be reversed by increasing dN supplementation (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Filamentous phenotypes have been documented under a range of stress conditions, including in the presence of β-lactam antibiotics.
source: Filamentous phenotypes have been documented under a range of stress conditions, including in the presence of β-lactam antibiotics (Stevenson et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2004; Yao et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The filamentous phenotype reduced over the course of the evolution experiment, suggesting that the lines were adapting to the scarcity of dNs.
source: Interestingly, we found that this phenotype reduced over the course of the experiment, suggesting that our lines were adapting to the scarcity of dNs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cell length measurements over the course of the evolution experiment.

claim: The DERA pathway has been considered a plausible ancestral route for the origin of DNA.
source: with some considering it to be a plausible ancestral route for the origin of DNA (Benner et al., 1989; Poole et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of ribonucleotide reduction does not lead to compensatory deoxyribonucleotide synthesis via the DERA pathway.
source: First, it indicates that loss of ribonucleotide reduction does not lead to compensatory deoxyribonucleotide synthesis via the DERA pathway
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental evolution data showing mutations in deoB rather than adaptation of the pathway for synthesis.

claim: Loss of phosphopentomutase function via mutation of deoB suggests that the DERA pathway is not readily accessible for synthesis of deoxyribonucleotides in vivo.
source: loss of phosphopentomutase function via mutation of deoB suggests that this pathway is not readily accessible for synthesis of deoxyribonucleotides in vivo
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental evolution data.

claim: Both acetaldehyde toxicity and low intracellular availability may preclude a simple switch to using the DERA pathway for dNTP production.
source: We note however that both acetaldehyde toxicity (to both DERA and cells more generally) and low intracellular availability may preclude a simple switch to using the DERA pathway for dNTP production (Ogawa et al., 2003; Poole et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and citations to published literature.

claim: Under conditions of severe dN restriction (0.01 mg/mL), parallel loss-of-function mutations at the deoB locus are observed.
source: In the second phase of our experiment, dN supplementation is dropped from 0.25 mg/mL to 0.01 mg/mL, and it is under these conditions of severe dN restriction that we observe parallel loss-of function mutations at the deoB locus (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data presented in Table 1.

claim: When deoxyribonucleotides are in short supply, deoB loss of function ensures that dNTPs are not lost to glycolysis via salvage.
source: We conclude that, when deoxyribonucleotides are in short supply, deoB loss of function ensures that dNTPs are not lost to glycolysis via salvage (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and understanding of the pathway, illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: deoB loss-of-function mutations serve to prevent dR loss to central metabolism while still permitting phosphorylase-mediated dN resynthesis.
source: Thus, deoB loss-of-function mutations serve to prevent dR loss to central metabolism while still permitting phosphorylase-mediated dN resynthesis (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and understanding of the pathway, illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: Loss of function of the DERA pathway is advantageous in the short term, precluding its cooption to deoxyribonucleotide synthesis.
source: Thus, while conversion of DERA to a synthetic pathway might be a better long-term solution to loss of ribonucleotide reduction, loss of function of this pathway is advantageous in the short term, precluding its cooption to deoxyribonucleotide synthesis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental evolution data.

claim: This interpretation is consistent with a recent experiment where mutation of dihydrofolate reductase led to deoB loss of function to prevent loss of deoxyribose-5-phosphate to glycolysis.
source: This interpretation is consistent with a recent experiment where mutation of dihydrofolate reductase led to deoB loss of function to prevent loss of deoxyribose-5-phosphate to glycolysis (Rodrigues and Shakhnovich, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Analysis of species that lack nrd genes reveals frequent loss of deoB, suggesting that loss of ribonucleotide reduction might drive loss of deoB.
source: Analysis of species that lack nrd genes reveals frequent loss of deoB, suggesting that loss of ribonucleotide reduction might drive loss of deoB, as observed in our experiments.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genome database searches and comparison with experimental results.

claim: All members of the genus Ureaplasma completely lack genes for ribonucleotide reduction and show no evidence of coding for either deoB or cdd.
source: For members of Ureaplasma, the pattern is clear (Supplementary file 1L): all members of this genus completely lack genes for ribonucleotide reduction and show no evidence of coding for either deoB or cdd
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST searches against Ureaplasma genome assemblies.

claim: Close to half of sequenced Buchnera strains show co-occurrence of ribonucleotide reduction and phosphopentomutase genes (48/74 strains).
source: Close to half of sequenced Buchnera strains show co-occurrence of ribonucleotide reduction and phosphopentomutase genes (48/74 strains)
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST searches against B. aphidicola genome assemblies.

claim: 30% (22/74 strains) of B. aphidicola lack genes for both ribonucleotide reduction and phosphopentomutase functions.
source: with 30% (22/74 strains) lacking genes for both functions (Supplementary file 1N)
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST searches against B. aphidicola genome assemblies.

claim: Loss of one function (RNR or deoB) may not always result in loss of the other in B. aphidicola.
source: If confirmed, this would indicate loss of one function may not always result in loss of the other.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genome analysis showing some strains with only one function lost.

claim: Members of the Borrelia lost deoB but retained ribonucleotide reduction.
source: This pattern could be taken to indicate that members of the Borrelia lost deoB but retained ribonucleotide reduction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genome analysis, though the authors note this interpretation is complicated by horizontal gene transfer.

claim: The class Ib RNR genes (nrdEF) in Borrelia have been acquired via horizontal gene transfer.
source: However, phylogenetic analyses (Zhong et al., 2006) and location on linear plasmids (Miller et al., 2013) indicate that the class Ib RNR genes (nrdEF) in Borrelia has been acquired via horizontal gene transfer
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on phylogenetic analyses and gene location.

claim: Class Ib RNR carried by members of the Borrelia is manganese-dependent.
source: It is noteworthy that class Ib RNR, carried by members of the Borrelia, is manganese-dependent (Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Class Ia RNR is an iron-dependent enzyme.
source: whereas class Ia is an iron-dependent enzyme (Torrents, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Borreliella burgdorferi does not require iron.
source: Interestingly, the most well-studied member of the Borreliaceae, Borreliella burgdorferi (sensu Adeolu and Gupta) does not require iron (Posey and Gherardini, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Initial loss of ribonucleotide reduction in Borreliaceae may have been driven by selection for iron independence, with subsequent reacquisition favouring the manganese-dependent enzyme.
source: It is tempting to speculate that initial loss of ribonucleotide reduction was driven by selection for iron independence, with subsequent reacquisition of ribonucleotide reduction favouring the manganese-dependent enzyme.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the data about RNR types and iron requirements.

claim: The switch to an intracellular existence may result in relaxed selection on ribonucleotide reduction if host-derived deoxyribonucleotides are sufficient to replace endogenous production.
source: More generally, the switch to an intracellular existence may result in relaxed selection on ribonucleotide reduction if host-derived deoxyribonucleotides are sufficient to replace endogenous production.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from evolutionary theory and the observed pattern of RNR loss in intracellular bacteria.

claim: Loss of ribonucleotide reduction appears to be an infrequent outcome as most intracellular bacteria retain ribonucleotide reduction.
source: This appears to be an infrequent outcome as most intracellular bacteria retain ribonucleotide reduction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the rarity of RNR loss in intracellular bacteria.

claim: In the absence of endogenous ribonucleotide reduction, disruption of the DERA pathway via mutations to deoB may serve to minimise loss of building blocks when dNTP availability is limited.
source: Our experiments indicate that, in the absence of endogenous ribonucleotide reduction, disruption of the DERA pathway via mutations to deoB may serve to minimise loss of these building blocks when dNTP availability is limited.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental evolution data.

claim: Life without ribonucleotide reduction drives the loss of dNTP catabolism via DERA, enabling building block reuse for DNA synthesis.
source: Given the necessity of genome replication, we conclude that life without ribonucleotide reduction drives the loss of dNTP catabolism via DERA, enabling building block reuse for DNA synthesis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and genome analysis of natural bacteria.

claim: Loss of ribonucleotide reduction appears extremely rare in the evolution of endosymbiosis and parasitism, despite the seeming ubiquity of host-derived deoxyribonucleotides.
source: It is interesting to note that loss of ribonucleotide reduction appears extremely rare in the evolution of endosymbiosis and parasitism, despite the seeming ubiquity of host-derived deoxyribonucleotides.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the rarity of RNR loss in intracellular bacteria.

claim: Many bacteria possess mechanisms for uptake of dNs, deoxyribonucleotides, and even DNA.
source: Acquisition from the host would appear straightforward as many bacteria are known to possess mechanisms for uptake of dNs, deoxyribonucleotides, and even DNA (Huang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: E. coli codes for two broad-spectrum nucleoside transporters, NupC and NupG, which have been reported to take up dNs.
source: E. coli for instance codes for two broad-spectrum nucleoside transporters, NupC and NupG, which have been reported to take up dNs (Patching et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Imported dNs may not be readily utilised in DNA synthesis as they must first be converted to deoxyribonucleotides for utilisation in genome synthesis.
source: It may be that imported dNs are not readily utilised in DNA synthesis as they must first be converted to deoxyribonucleotides for utilisation in genome synthesis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the requirement for heterologous kinase expression to enable RNR deletion.

claim: It was only possible to eliminate ribonucleotide reduction after first introducing a broad-spectrum deoxyadenosine kinase gene from M. mycoides.
source: In our experiments, it was only possible to eliminate ribonucleotide reduction after first introducing a broad-spectrum deoxyadenosine kinase gene from M. mycoides
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing unsuccessful deletion attempts without the kinase.

claim: The M. mycoides deoxyadenosine kinase presumably improves the opportunity for imported dNs to be coopted for deoxyribonucleotide synthesis instead of being catabolised.
source: presumably because it improves the opportunity for imported dNs to be coopted for deoxyribonucleotide synthesis instead of being catabolised.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental requirement for the kinase.

claim: dNs, deoxyribonucleotides, and DNA can all be used as a nitrogen source by E. coli.
source: Indeed, a recent study shows that dNs, deoxyribonucleotides, and DNA can all be used as a nitrogen source by E. coli (Huang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Under conditions where DNA and its monomeric building blocks are important sources of nitrogen and phosphorus, loss of ribonucleotide reduction would presumably have a deleterious impact on growth.
source: Thus, under conditions where DNA and its monomeric building blocks are important sources of nitrogen and phosphorus, loss of ribonucleotide reduction would presumably have a deleterious impact on growth.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the role of the DERA pathway in catabolism.

claim: This trade-off may explain the small number of instances of loss of ribonucleotide reduction.
source: This trade-off may explain the small number of instances of loss of ribonucleotide reduction.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the competing demands of dNTP synthesis and catabolism.

claim: The reverse DERA pathway may be favoured under conditions where other nitrogen and phosphorous sources are abundant.
source: It remains to be seen whether there are conditions wherein the reverse DERA pathway (Poole et al., 2014) can operate synthetically in vivo as an alternative to ribonucleotide reduction, but one possibility is that this may be favoured under conditions where other nitrogen and phosphorous sources are abundant.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential conditions for DERA pathway operation.

claim: E. coli B strain REL606 was used as the wild-type strain for all experiments.
source: E. coli B strain REL606 (Lenski et al., 1991) was used as the wild-type strain for all experiments.
evidence: The claim is a statement of experimental methods.

claim: REL606 is well suited for experimental evolution, having been subjected to a long-running evolution experiment.
source: We elected to perform experiments using REL606 as it is well suited for experimental evolution, having been subjected to a long-running evolution experiment (Lenski et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: REL606 has genomically coded resistance against streptomycin.
source: Two key features that make this strain convenient for such work are genomically coded resistance against streptomycin
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the REL606 strain.

claim: REL606 has a selectively neutral mutation in the araA gene, making it easy to detect via colony colour when grown on tetrazolium arabinose.
source: and a selectively neutral mutation in the araA gene, making it easy to detect via colony colour when grown on tetrazolium arabinose.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the REL606 strain.
